utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start with the next witness, very briefly, a few procedural matters. I was informed that there was something with D15777, a new page uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. I believe there's no objection, and the new page 3 is 1D70 -- excuse me, 1D70-8586 which is the new page 3 for D1577.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes and new page is -- you had a better one or it was a translation [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a completed translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a complete translation of the document, the English translation. That's what we're ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all. In the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We just received this an hour or so ago. We'll just check it and make sure that that was the issue. I think there was a translation issue with one of the pages. We'll just check it and get back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can correct counsel. I don't think there was a full translation and the whole thing is translated now, but can you check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hedaraly, if we do not hear from you later today, could we assume that there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, because, I think D1577 was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, it remains admitted evidence and if there's any problem with it, we'd like to hear from you not later than today. Second issue. After the recess, the Chamber intends to return to five days of sitting a week. We'll closely monitor how this works out. The problem is not primarily in this case, but it'S the combination with another case on which two of the Judges of this Bench are sitting. Then the Chamber recently received a 92 bis application for 11 statements. Now, if only for scheduling purposes, the Chamber would very much appreciate if it could receive already a provisional point of view from the Prosecution before the recess starts, because, if there would be a strong opposition against these witnesses to be called without cross-examination, then the Chamber would decide on the basis of that decide that all witnesses would be called to be cross-examined and make them all 92 ter witnesses, that, of course, would have quite some impact on scheduling. So, therefore, the Chamber would appreciate if a provisional response, I'm not asking you to -- to give it in detail but just to say, Well, majority or almost all of them we would agree with admission under 92 bis or for a majority we would still seek the witness to be called for cross-examination, so something of the kind so that we are not taken by surprise after the recess. Those were the procedural matters I would like to raise. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we move into private session briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Kehoe, is the Prosecution [sic] ready to call its next witness, which is -- there are no protective measures sought, which is Mr. Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think the Defence is ready, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You see, it's really --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's vacation time, Judge. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher is doing her duties appropriately and is escorting the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be General Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, the rules require to you make a solemn declaration. You have the text already in your hands, could you please make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Cross. Mr. Cross, when I address you by "mister" rather than by title, it is not in any way out of disrespect. That's the way the Chamber addresses all witnesses appearing before it, whatever their function or title is. Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- examine Mr. Cross. Mr. Cross, Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. General Gotovina, and he will be the first one to examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, can you state your name for the record and spell your last name?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: My name is Timothy Cross, C-r-o-s-s, as in "sugar."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And now, General Cross, can you just give us your years of service in the British army and the date you retired and the rank you held upon retirement?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Sure. I joined the army cadets, actually, 1964. Went to an army college in 1967. I went to the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst and was commissioned into the British army in 1971, and I retired in January 2007 in the rank of Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General Cross, I'd like to show you the report that you have submitted in this cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could bring up 65 ter 1D2741 and if I could ask the assistance of the usher if the witness can have a hard copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, looking at this document, do you recognise this as the report that you filed in this cause?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And turning to the -- it should be page 24 in e-court. And that would be your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you recognise that as your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we are not going go into that curriculum vitae and all items of your background, General, but I would like to just discuss a few items in your career that are pertinent to the hearing that we have hear today, if I may. Now, just going chronologically on some of your deployments - and I start with your deployment in Northern Ireland - and when was that, sir, and what type of operation was it, and what role did you have in that operation?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: In 1978 I deployed to Northern Ireland as a captain. I was a part of a small unit that was looking after all of the ammunition aspects of Northern Ireland, including the bomb disposal work in Northern Ireland, and I ran the -- what's called the ammunition inspectorate, and that took me around the province looking at all aspects of the ammunition, including ammunition that was handed in by the public which had to be disposed of, dealing with terrorists, and improvised explosive devices, and examining and producing reports on the ammunition that was stored by the British Army throughout the province.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cross. It is only now that the French translation was able to finish its translation, because it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will speak a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- slow down a bit. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, specifically that's your role, but what exactly was going on with the British army in Northern Ireland during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: In 1969 there were what became known as the troubles in Northern Ireland. This was largely the Catholic minority who were protesting in various ways, and that became so serious that the government decided to deploy the British Army to Northern Ireland in support of civil authority. It's an operation which is called "Military Assistance to the Civil Power." And we deployed a number of troops early in 1969/1970 whilst I was still at Sandhurst at the time being commissioned, and those troops were there to help restore security to Northern Ireland which would give the space and the time to the politicians to try to resolve the problems within the Catholic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go chronologically General to your next deployment, I believe your CV reflects that you were in Cyprus thereafter. Can you tell us a little bit background in that regard what the British Army was doing, what type of operation it was, and what specifically you were doing?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes, Cyprus was at the time -- well, Cyprus, of course, at one stage had been a British -- part of the British colonial rule, and we retrain two sovereign republic bases in Cyprus. There had been trouble between the Greeks and Turks over Cyprus for some time, and in 1974 Turkey had invaded the northern part of the island. There was an UN observer force in Cyprus at that time, it became what was known as the UN force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, and it was a UN peace-keeping force that was deployed. It consisted of a number of different nations. The British provided a battalion to help monitor the line between the Greek and Turkish half of the island, and we also provided a number of officers or soldiers to the headquarters of UNFICYP based in Nicosia. I was a captain and deployed to take command of the ordnance detachment within the support regiment of the UNFICYP headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next item I'd just like to chat with you briefly about was the Gulf war in the early 1990s. Again, could you replicate your explanation with regard to what the British army was doing, what type of operation it was, and what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I was serving in Germany. I had just taken over command of a battalion, so I was now a lieutenant-colonel. I had deployed to Germany in September of 1990, which coincided with the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq. The British government along with others, of course, decided to deploy some assets to Iraq. We initially deployed a brigade in September, October, November, and then in December it was decided to reinforce that commitment with a divisional headquarters, a second brigade, and a large number of supporting combat power. I deployed as part of the divisional headquarters. I was the commander of the supply support for the division, and I deployed to Al Jubail [phoen] in December of 1995 and stayed through until we left in -- I think it was April 1996, once Iraq had left Kuwait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now turning to the Balkans. General, I believe you had several deployments at various levels in the Balkans. Can we just go through those briefly?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995, the Dalton -- not the Dalton, the Dayton, Dayton Peace Accord had been signed. We, the UK, had already deployed some troops as part the UN protection force in the Balkans in the early 1990s, what was known as UNPROFOR, and after Dayton we agreed to deploy a divisional headquarters and other assets to help implement Dayton under what was known as the implementation force or IFOR. At this stage, I was a full colonel, and I deployed as the commander of a logistic support, force support, for that UK deployment. That took me in through Split and the division deployed up to Kupres, and Sipovo and other places in the middle of Bosnia. I left there after some months and came back. I took over command of a brigade in 1997 in the Balkans. I went back to the Balkans to take over command of my brigade. My brigade headquarters was deployed at this stage in various places throughout Croatia and Bosnia. And I stayed there for a tour with what was then called the sustainment fours for the Balkans or SFOR. I then came background there from after six months or so, continued to command the brigade in the United Kingdom, and then deployed to the Balkans, this time for the Kosovo deployment known as KFOR. At which stage, again I was a brigade commander. We deployed through Thessaloniki in Greece and moved both my brigade and another brigade into Macedonia. This was on the assumption that the peace talks that were happening in Rambouillet at the time would produce probably, we thought, the equivalent of a Dayton Accord. And the UK government, and indeed ourselves, believed that we would see that accord signed and we would then move up into Kosovo to conduct a similar operation to IFOR. As the Court will know that Rambouillet did not succeed, the talks did not succeed, and so NATO began a different campaign, and I stayed with that deployment through until eventually I left the following August, and we had been involved in various aspects of that deployment which you may or may not wish to ask about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, we can go into that a bit when we start discussing some of the substance of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just cover one last item. And that is your deployment in Baghdad with the Office of Reconstruction and Humanitarian Affairs, ORHA?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which ultimately became as we know the Coalition Provisional Authority or CPA. Could you just talk to us just a bit about that and your role in that?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: This began in 2002 for me, I won't go through the politics of the run up to this, but around October 2002 I was told by the chief of the General Staff, the British chief of the General Staff, that he wanted me to establish a headquarters known as a joint force logistic component headquarters. This would be a two star headquarters, a headquarters commanded by a Major-General, which is what at this stage my rank was, and that involved me establishing the headquarters within the United Kingdom but also travelling to the American headquarters in Tampa in Florida called CENTCOM where General Franks and his headquarters were planning for possible operations in Iraq. This, of course, had followed on September the 11th and American forces had been in Afghanistan, initial deployment, and they were now planning for possible operations in Iraq. As the logistic component commander I travelled to Tampa on several occasions, and with my other component commanders were looking at the British contribution and possible involvement in that deployment. Around Christmas time, the UK government, as a result of various conversations decided -- came to the conclusion that our engagement in that possible conflict would change. Until that time we had assumed that wee -- if it had become necessary, we would enter Iraq from the north and we would deploy through the eastern Mediterranean ports along a long line of communication and then enter Iraq through the north with an American division and that our role would be to secure the northern oil fields and the towns around Krukut [phoen] and elsewhere, the north of Iraq, the Kurdish region. The British government having concluded that the Turkish government would not wish us to do that made the decision that we would indeed go south and work with the American forces in the south. Logistically that was a much easier operation. At the time I was commanding under my command were two logistics brigades and a number of other assets, and as a result of this change, the UK reduced the logistic commitment to a single logistic brigade. I therefore handed over responsibility for the logistic component command to a one star level brigadier, what some nations call brigadier general, and I returned to an appointment that I had held before this began. Two weeks later I was rung up by the chief of the General Staff, and told that he wished me to go to Washington, to join a small planning team which was led at the time by a man called Jay Garner, who was a retired military -- US military officer, lieutenant-general, and this was at the time called the Office of Post-War Planning. This office had been established under a presidential directive in January of 2003. I joined them in early February 2003, and I stayed with that team in the transition to what became known as ORHA, as you have said; eventually became the Coalition Provisional Authority. I worked with them in Washington, deployed to Kuwait in the spring, and then went into Baghdad at the fall of Baghdad, with that headquarters, and I left Iraq at the end of June 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to clarify one acronym that you used, General. You noted CENTCOM in Tampa, that's central command, is it not?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to talk a little bit initially about these two roles that you had in the Iraq situation starting first with your role as a component commander, and then in your role working with General Garner in the Office of Post-War Planning or the office of ORHA, the Office of Reconstruction and Humanitarian Assistance. Now in page -- I best -- I believe it's page 9 of your statement, you talk a bit about this role as a component commander basically in paragraph 35, but I think it's the third line down or second line down in paragraph 35. Can you tell us a little bit, General, about what this means when you refer to a component commander?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: When the United Kingdom deploy military operations, they plan the deployment within the United Kingdom in a permanent headquarters based near London and with the Ministry of Defence they appointed a commander for that deployment. He is normally a three-star lieutenant-general equivalent -- or equivalent rank, so it could be an airman or a maritime officer, a royal naval office, or an army lieutenant-general. That three-star appointment who commands the deployment is known as the joint task Force Commander, and he is in overall command of that deployment. We then appoint five component commanders, an air component commander, an air officer of two-star rank, a maritime component commander, a royal naval officer of two-star rank, a land component commander, a Major-General, normally one of our divisional commanders. A logistic component commander, depending on the size of the operation that might be a one star or a brigadier general or two star major-general rank, in my case for this deployment to Iraq it was a two-star rank, and finally a commander of our special forces. So there are five component commanders working to the Joint Task Force Commander. We deployed them in different way. Normally on these operations when we're working with, particularly the US forces, we will often put our component commanders in the same headquarters as their equivalents for the US, but not always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I consulted with my colleagues to know the details of how planning was made in military areas does not in any way assist the Chamber in the determinations it will have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will get to the point of this. I will short-circuit this if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you have in the workup an operational commander, an overall operation commander; for instance, in Iraq, is there not?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe in this case it was General Franks?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you mentioned for us that you had a retired general, General Garner, that was responsible for the post conflict work in Iraq; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you have an operational commander who is, like General Franks, getting ready to conduct this war, is he part of this planning going on for the post conflict situation that General Garner was taking care of and that ultimately you were taking care of, or is there a division of responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: In the example you're quoting, General Franks was the operational commander for the military deployment to Iraq. General Garner is appointed to a separate office of post war planning. His headquarters was based inside the Pentagon in Washington. General Franks' headquarters was in Tampa, Florida, as we said earlier. Now, there is a linkage between them in that, obviously, there is a transition from purely military operations to the reconstruction of any nation or area of operations post-conflict. But essentially, it is Garner's headquarters who is trying to pull together the plan for post-conflict reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would it be General Franks who is getting ready to plan and conduct the war, and General Garner who is getting ready for the post-conflict activity in Iraq?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you talk in your report - and I'm referring to some of your discussions in -- from paragraph 47 to 54, and we are not going to go through all of that - but we would -- you talk about the what the end state is and you explain what the general end state is, what you're trying to accomplish. And I believe you say that the offensive campaign - would the offensive campaign and the peace support operations be two components of that, whatever the end state happens to be, working towards that end state?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I should stress that the expression "end state" is relatively new in doctrinal terms, but it attempts to encapsulate what it is that this operation is intended to bring about, the changes, what we want this place to look like once this operation is over. And in most cases, indeed one would could argue in all cases, that is not a military end state. It is it much broader and bigger than that. So, for example in Iraq and indeed in Afghanistan, the end state is something about establishing a free nation that is at peace with itself and its neighbour, establishing democracy, a number of expresses that people will bring together to say this is what we would like this nation to look like once this is over. Within that end state there are a lot of different organisations, a lot of different players who will be a key part of bringing that about. And the military's role is obviously to engage in military operations should they be necessary, either in offensive operations and war fighting, or, as I referred to earlier, to conduct peace support operations if there had been an agreement prior to the move-in. And having conducted those operations, to then establish the secure environment within which the non-military players will then bring about this complete end state. So, for example, the military would be responsible for securing the environment that would then enable the judicial system to be established. And I could give some examples of that if you would wish me to go into it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please turn off all unnecessary microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Not guilty, Your Honour. So they would be responsible for establishing a judicial system, and there would be people responsible for establishing an education system or a trade system. Those people would come perhaps from a variety of different organisations, so in the Balkans, there were various players, non-military players, involved in that work the EU, the OSCE, the United Nations, a lot of non-governmental organisations who would all be responsible for delivering parts of that requirement to deliver that end state. So being clear what it is you're trying to achieve is quite important, if not very important, because then you understand what needs to be done, and indeed you understand that when that has been achieved this operation has been overall successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, just, if I may, referring to your statement, and I think you alluded to this to some degree in paragraph 48 in the second-to-last line -- or third-to-last line, "It is important to note that the military and all its resources are only one component of the total resources of the state that will be required to achieve an end state."

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: That is correct. And those other components can be made up of other --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please turn off the unnecessary microphones thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can be made up of other state actors, but also as I've noted, non-governmental state actors as well, so NGOs who help with the humanitarian issues and international organisations under the umbrella of United Nations, perhaps, who will be helping to be deliver some aspects of that end state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned to us the set up of a court system. I trust that's one of the component elements that you are referring to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes. If I may just refer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may just refer to the attachment 3 that I included with my statement, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that's -- if I may, General, that's on the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yeah. Essentially, what that attachment is trying to show is that the constituent parts of any nation, nation building, post-conflict nation building, has to encompass all of these, in this example, cords of a rope, and the military is shown as a single cord here, but the rule of law is a separate cord of this rope. And that rule of law of course is not necessarily unique but certainly will apply to that nation. So the rule of law in the Balkans might be different in the way that the constitution is constructed to other operations around the world. It may be that some military assets are used to assist in that process, but it is not the military whose role is to establish that rule of law, policing, judiciary, prison service, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page of this report to just view this for on moment, the cord that you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can spin that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, in there you talk about the constituent's military being one of them, and you not the array of other components. Now, discussing resources and those components, and I ask this question on the strategic as opposed to the operational level, when a decision is made on resources to be provided to all these constituent components, is that done on a strategic or an operational level?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: It would be done --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be done primarily at the strategic level. So, for example, when we were preparing to move into Baghdad, both for the for the United Kingdom and indeed for United States and other nations who were engaged at that time, there were people being nominated from other departments, other governmental departments, to deploy alongside the military to take the lead in standing up the ministries, standing up the education system, and so on. For the United Kingdom we deployed people from our Foreign Office, people from our Department of International development, and indeed capabilities from the police, the Home Office, and others. The United States and indeed other nations deployed individuals from within their treasury departments, from within their health departments, from within their education departments, an array of individual who would be responsible for various aspects and indeed the many subconstituent parts within each one of these cords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I'd like to go into the central focus of your report which is post-conflict matters, and peace support planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And for the Chamber and all those in courtroom, we'll be referring for the most part between paragraph 55 to 79, and if we can start at the outset, General, with a comment that you make in paragraph 56, and it's four lines down: "That said, the lessons of history reveal that certain problems and challenges can invariably be expected in post-conflict areas." General, can you just elaborate briefly on that -- what you are trying to say in that -- what you were -- just explain what you were trying to say.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Every -- this is obviously my personal story in the sense of the different deployments that have I been involved with over the years. Every one of those deployments is unique. It's not possible to produce a template, a solution that can be applied in every deployment. What is suitable for the Balkans, for example, might not be suitable for Iraq or indeed a deployment to Africa or somewhere else in the world, and indeed what is suitable for a particular part of the world at one period of time may not be suitable subsequently as events unfurl and things change. The reality, that said, is that there are certainly problems and events that reoccur on these deployments. When there have been -- when there's been a war, when people have been at each other's throats for a long period of time, in many cases many years, over many years, indeed in some cases over many generations, then retribution, criminality, chaos, you know, is an inevitable consequence in my experience. So what we saw happening in Kosovo, once the KFOR had deployed into Kosovo, what we saw happening in Baghdad is not unusual, not unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us stay with that. Those two items as we hear, and talk to us a little bit about what you saw happening in Kosovo on your KFOR deployment?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I think it might be helpful to just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be helpful to just lay out from my personal point of view the run-up to the move into Kosovo. Notwithstanding what I was explaining earlier, as a result of the NATO bombing of Serbia, the numbers of the internally displaced persons within Kosovo who then subsequently crossed over the borders into Macedonia and Albania and therefore became refugees, those numbers incrossed dramatically over this period. For various reasons which I'm very happy to explain, my brigade ended up by building and running refugee camps because there were not sufficient non-governmental aid agencies, or indeed UN agencies, in the region to do that. So I saw and worked alongside and operated the refugee camps in northern Macedonia, in southern Albania, for some time before we moved into Kosovo. Once agreement had been reached for KFOR to move into Kosovo, the original thinking was that there would be a sort of orderly return of all of these refugee who had crossed over the international borders and that KFOR would try and organise various aspects of -- of the infrastructure and so on within Kosovo before these people came back. What happened was the minute the border was opened, the refugee camps that I had built and operated, which contained several tens of thousands of refugees, virtually emptied over night. Over two or three days, everybody just started returning. So the first thing that happens is that people want to go back to their homes, to their villages, to their towns, or indeed the cities, like Pristina, and trying to do that in an orderly way, it's always -- I wouldn't wanted to be too specific, but my personal view is always virtually impossible. People, not surprisingly, want to get back to their home villages and so on. In many cases, of course, they had been separated from members of their families. Most of the refugees in Macedonia were elderly or were women and children. A lot of men had either been killed within Kosovo in the previous years or they had gone into the hills and joined the Kosovo Liberation Army, the KLA, or indeed had disappeared. So families wanted to be reunited with their fathers, their uncles, their brothers, or, indeed, their children, and we did have quite a few families in the camps who had just children on the way as they had been forced over out of their homes and forced over the border. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let me stop you right there just so I can ask one question. On this orderly return, why didn't you just set up check-points and control this return of these refugees going back to their homes? Was that a viable solution.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: From our point of view - and I say from our point of view, from a military point of view - we, of course, wished to ensure that the main roads, the main lines of communication, were kept open for the movement of the military and, of course, all of the supply chain requirements. And monitoring the flow of traffic up those main routes, in this case in Kosovo is there is only one main road from -- from Skopje to Pristina, alongside it there is a railway line, which we also established got up and running and used for these purposes, but essentially one wants to ensure that the military line of communication is kept relatively free, and so establishing check-points to try and control the flow of traffic using military police to do that is certainly something that we wanted to do and in some cases established. But, of course, these people came from their homes. They had -- there were lots of minor roads, lots of tracks, lots of routes through hills and the forests that got them back to their homes without using main roads, and any attempt to secure, if you like, the border area, and force people simply to use the main lines of communication, well, again, would be very difficult if not impossible and would certainly mean the use of a large amount of man power. In Northern Ireland, for example, and I say this in my statement, securing the border between the north of Ireland and the south of Ireland was something we worked hard to do, to stop the infiltration of weapons and other people and so forth. We established many vehicle check-points, many patrols and so on, but it is just impossible to seal a border in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continuing on with your observations and what you saw in KFOR as people began to move back into Kosovo. Can you explain that a bit?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think the -- there are a number of things that were going on. One of the things that is most noticeable is that very quickly small businesses spring up all over the place so that people are selling literally jugs of petrol, bottles of petrol, by the side of the road, packets of cigarettes, and so on. Where they get that from is debatable, but certainly essentially, to use the expression free enterprise, if you like, capitalism is trying to break out, people are trying to establish businesses and they are trying to secure a living. In going back to their homes and to their villages, one of the sadnesses for me, in Northern Ireland, in Cyprus, in the Balkans, Iraq, is that people turn to criminality and they turn to retribution. They try and find out who it was that threw them out of their homes in the first place. Maybe somebody who had killed members of their family, mass graves, of course, are found this these places, people try to find out who is accountable for that. And there is a very difficult line for the authorities to hold between doing that in a to formal coordinated controlled way and just banditry and criminality breaking out. In Kosovo, there was no doubt that there was a retribution going on, the Serb families that had stayed behind were intimidated and KFOR worked hard to stop that intimidation and to secure the areas and to try and establish the rule of law in and around, but that is extremely difficult to do and there is no doubt that there were murders and other things going on whilst KFOR initially moved into and then established itself. It is -- we're saying, of course, that in moving into these places there is a period of time when the military are establishing themselves as much as anything else. They are getting their bases sorted and so on, but very quickly you would be want to be seeing patrols out and about and gathering as much information as possible, and then attempting to bring, establish the secure environment that I spoke of earlier on, that would then enable the non-military players to bring proper reconstruction and reconciliation and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 34, you note in paragraph 32 about the chaos inherent in these situations and the types of crime were not unexpected, but you note in paragraph 34 that there were 50.000 KFOR troops, and it took between the 12th of July until -- in August of 19 -- excuse me, 12th of June and August, and I believe in paragraph 82 you say it took six to eight weeks. General, with that type of force of 55.000 -- 50.000 troops, why did it take this period of time to get this situation under control?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I think it is worth stressing that the total force of the KFOR --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's worth stressing that the 50.000 figure is roughly the size of KFOR and that includes, of course, headquarters and support structures and support units, but nonetheless we're talking probably effectively 30.000 to 40.000 troops who very quickly you wish to get out and about driving in their vehicles, finding out what's going on, trying to establish a secure environment. The reality is that you can't be everywhere all the time, and certainly you can't be guarding every building, and protecting every village. You try and establish a presence. You make it absolutely clear to people that force will be used, if necessary, to stop looting and violence and so on. In a situation like Dayton and IFOR this was relatively unnecessary, and very quickly the other agencies that we spoke of were able to impose and bring about the environment, the court system, the prison system, the economic development and so forth, but, as we know, sadly, in Baghdad that was not the case, and in Kosovo - although people worked very hard to establish that quickly - it did take a certain period of time to do so. I don't know, and I need to be careful in terms of these time-lines and what was going on in terms of the amount of criminality and the individual events that happened, my statement is intended to show that it did take a period of time for KFOR to establish that secure environment, and in my experience that is always the case. I think it is worth saying, too, that, of course, in any environment, in any city in the world, there is always criminality. That's why we have a police force, so one never gets rid of criminality. The important issue is that people understand that criminality will be discovered, investigated, people will be brought to justice, and there is an establishment of the rule of law, and although KFOR made that very clear from the beginning, it took a period of time before we were able to impose that and make it absolutely clear to people that criminality would not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with KFOR, General, at paragraph 73 at the top with the 50.000 troops, from 30.00 to 40.000 on the ground, you note that: "Operation Banner and KFOR had, in my opinion, sufficient 'boots on the ground' to succeed - over time - in stabilising their areas of responsibility." So looking back, General, with that type of reference, the six to eight weeks, do you consider that KFOR was successful after this period of time and with a sufficient amount of troops to stabilise the area?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Inevitably that is a matter of judgement. I would argue that Kosovo was ultimately successful and Northern Ireland was successful, but it doesn't mean to say - and I think again it is important to acknowledge - notwithstanding -- notwithstanding the fact that I don't take pleasure in acknowledging it, but in Northern Ireland for decades people were killed, there were riots on the streets at occasional seasons, known as the marching season in Northern Ireland, and indeed in Kosovo for some considerable period after this time, there were incidents that occurred which is why the military capability continued to be deployed in Kosovo, and indeed continued to deploy throughout the Balkans for a number of years and some aspects of it remains today. The -- the balance here is how much of a presence do you need to retain and sustain over time in order to sustain and maintain the secure environment, and I won't go into great detail, but there is one problem which in some places, if you keep military there too long they can become a part of the problem, and so you're constantly trying to keep the military reducing, in a way, and allow the civil establishments, civilian policing and so forth to be established, and that is a difficult balance. But I would argue, yes, Northern Ireland over time, but it was a long time. One has to acknowledge that Operation Banner was in place for 37 years in Northern Ireland. It started the year I was at Sandhurst, it finished the year I left the British Army, and Kosovo continued to be a difficult place for some considerable time after my deployment. But over all, the rule of law was pretty well in place for -- for that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with one last question on Kosovo. In -- you talk about some of the criminality that you observed in paragraphs 30 to 31, 32 of your report, and I would like to just focus you on the paragraph 32. The third -- fourth to last line: "The perpetrators ranged from desperate refugees to organised criminal elements including, I suspect, low level members of the KLA ..." General with regard to these KLA member, I mean, United Nations Mission in Kosovo, UNMIK, was essentially responsible for this area -- was responsible for the area, why didn't UNMIK or, in conjunction with NATO, just go in and remove these KLA leaders whose soldiers might have been committing some type of crime? Why didn't they do that?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I should say, I think, in response to that question, that that sort of decision was -- would have been taken certainly above my position. So General Mike Jackson who was a lieutenant-general in command of KFOR and the other national components and their governments would have certainly been involved in such a discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cross, sorry to interrupt you. The question was why they didn't do that. Do you know why they didn't do that, because you start now describing at what level such decisions would be taken. Do you know why they did not do that? If so, please tell. If you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly Your Honour. I think to be fair the answer to the question is I don't know specifically, but having lived through the experience, my understanding was that removing the senior command cohort would not have made a different to what we are talking about here. So the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my assessment, but I was not involved in the decision-making process. I'm not even sure, to be honest, whether there was a discussion about the necessity to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with your assessment, sir, based on the situation, why do you think it wouldn't have made a difference?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: The evidence that I saw, the evidence that I saw as I travelled around Kosovo, was that much of what was happening was not done as a result of specific orders being passed through a chain of command. There was no effective chain of command in many respects. Now, again I have not seen any evidence or construct within the KLA command chain, but many of the people who were returning to their villages and towns, as I said earlier, came from the refugee camps. Many of the people who'd headed for the hills inside Kosovo were ordinary people from these villages and towns, and they were returning back to them. I'm not aware that they were under any specific orders to do anything. They just went home, and in going home and got back to their villages, they then established their homes and their livelihoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on that, sir, these people that went up to the hills, did they, based on your knowledge, join up with the KLA while they were up in the hills?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Certainly some did, but I about not suggest by any means that all did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I'd like to just shift gears, if I may, and turn to some of the assumed facts that you were looking at in paragraph, and that would begin on page 18, and I'm most interested with regard to the paragraph (w) and (y) which discusses the amount of military police and civilian police. And while we -- in paragraph (z), which is the civilian police and in the operative area --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, and we did inform the Prosecution of this, with regard to paragraph (z) we have sent to the witness a -- updated figures and, of course, these are approximations because they don't squarely follow between the indictment and Sector South, but we provided a information in D1577 and approximated the level of civilian police to somewhere in the area of 700 to 800 as opposed to the 400 to 500 figure, and we did that based on the testimony of a recent witness that came after the General had -- or we filed a report on the General's behalf. So I just wanted to advise the court of that as we move through this, that we have actually upgraded that number. Once again, it doesn't squarely fall between Sector South and the indictment time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to correct that the information we received was that that number was up to 700, not 800, and it was I believe not confirmed by the witness, it was an exhibit D1577. So just so that the record is clear, that's the information we received from the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the purpose, of course, is to put it in that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... is that challenged? Mr. Hedaraly give as small correction to what you said. Any challenge to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we were just trying to use the highest number possible which was 700 to 800, so I mean if we can go with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Let's try to come to what perhaps should be the core of the evidence of this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, just looking at these particular figures in (w) and (z), and as a preliminary question, this Chamber has received evidence, and this is at D1361, at page 21, paragraph 147, that approximately 42.000 ethnic Croats who were internally displaced people from Sector South alone, that was the number, and likewise have received information that people were attempting to come back. Without repeating what you said before, in detail, would such a coming back of the civilian population into Sector South after Operation Storm present security concerns as you've addressed?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes. I think 42.000 is significantly large figure and trying to control that flow would not be easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as you were preparing your report, were you aware of some of the events that had taken place that would lead to degrees of recrimination and revenge from the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: In what context?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of the people who had been expelled and were now returning?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: And we're talking here of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In Kosovo as the -- and is the parallel with Croatia, coming into the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Again, I must stress this is a personal judgement, but from my experiences of all the interethnic and various other deployments I have been involved with, the sad reality is that as people return bark, yes, they -- they are involved in various aspects of criminality, and I remember saying to, when we were building refugee camps in northern Macedonia, having to explain to people, particularly the media, that within these camps there were people who were angry and had had relatives killed, and they were not innocent in the sense that they were -- this was a sample of humanity here who had gone through very difficult times, and it was quite clear that however hard we tried it was going to be difficult, if not extremely difficult, to stop the sort of things that you're alluding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could we just have a clarification on whether -- the question was whether the witness was aware of that criminality, and I think the witness is referring to his awareness of what happened in Kosovo. If we can just clarify, because the question has the "to" and the answer is combines. If we could just clarify that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I can only comment on what I have experienced and seen in Kosovo. I was not aware of what was happening in -- in this part of the Balkans in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although usually the Chamber decides on what to do with objections, and requests for further clarification, Mr. Cross. You have directly responded. I would invite you not to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I will wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think it certainly is not dramatic, at this moment, Mr. Kehoe, was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, before we move off this point, from your experience in the Balkans were you aware what happened to the Croats in the Krajina from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. But not in -- in great detail. I had not been involved in the UN deployment to the Balkans. I had been through the Gulf campaign that I spoke of, and I continued to command my regiment in Germany. When we deployed as part of the NATO implementation force in 1995, we deployed the British forces through Split, through the port of Split, the airhead was in Split, and the shipping that we deployed in the theatre came through Split north port, and we took the equipment by road from Split across into Bosnia through the Kamensko crossing by road, so -- moving through that area listening to people talking to people, I was aware of the fact that there had been this trouble in the years that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I consulted with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I look at your last question, that is the question of a kind of -- from your experience as being a European, were you aware of what happened between 1940 and 1945 in Europe. These are unfocussed questions which do not assist the Chamber. The Chamber invites you to come to the core of what, apparently, is -- was on the mind of the Gotovina Defence when it selected this witness. Until now, if five per cent or seven per cent has even come close to that, that might be a relatively high estimate. Would you please not provide the Chamber -- of course, we do understand that the experience of the witness in Iraq and Kosovo, et cetera, is relevant for the experience on which he bases his expert opinion. But to ask the witness to tell a lot about what happened in Kosovo and what happened in Iraq and then say, Well, could you please compare that with Croatia, well, apparently the witness has relatively little knowledge about that, doesn't assist at this moment, the Chamber. Would you please keep this in mind, and could I ask you how much time had you in mind to continue the examination of this witness. By the way, the report is quite clear. That's another perhaps small problem, that quite a lot of your questions are dealt with in the report in such a way that it's clear to the Chamber what the witness wants to convey to us and what you ask him does not always add much to that. Could you tell us on how much time you would still need so that I can consider that, together with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, there are -- I do look forward to the opportunity to tying this all together to you and alleviating the Court's impatience. With regard to the -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no impatience by this Court, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please -- do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't accept that, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. That's on the record now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with regard to the focus of this, of course, we never got a 94 -- a Rule 94 bis focus as to what the Prosecution was disagreeing with in this score, so -- I mean, I've attempted to outline the general parameters of what the witness is saying for the purposes of the Trial Chamber, given the fact that the Prosecution has simply said orally last week that they wanted to cross-examine the witness. So, I will attempt to focus this as quickly as possible under these circumstances, Mr. President. I do not believe that I have taken an inadequate period of time. We started approximately one hour ago with this witness. I had listed it for three hours, and I will be done relatively briefly, and there is the basis of my conclusions in that regard, and once again, it's -- it's simply a matter of receiving from the Trial Chamber what was given to the Prosecution. And simply we will get through this very quickly with these matters, but the Gotovina Defence concluded that it was essential to bring certain elements of this to the Court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back, General, to paragraph 80, and with the assumed facts that had been set forth, we have 1.000 military police and 3.500 civilian police for the entire Krajina. Based on your experience, General, in Northern Ireland, in Cyprus, in Kosovo, and in Baghdad, with those resources would you have expected a high degree of control in that area given the facts that we've talked about, such as 32.000 civilians coming back, and there being a transition with the HV taking this area back from the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: If I may, I think I would respond but saying I think it's important to say that the -- it's not just the numbers we're talking about here. It's the quality and the professionalism of the people. The numbers to me, from what I have seen in the other places, are certainly low in -- in assuming that they could bring order out of a very chaotic situation. If -- if they were moving into an area that was calm and all that was required from normal policing, and if these were professional policemen who were well led and had a strong ethic and ethos of establishing justice and fairness and so forth in the way that we would all expect and desire of our police forces, then that be would one issue. I do think it's important to recognise that the ability to command, control, and give a construct to these people, I have no way of knowing what that was like. I have no way of knowing what, to use a military term, the morale component of these people was like, what was their leadership like, what was the command and control structure like, what was their ethics, what was their ethos, did they understand and apply, for the military, the laws of armed conflict, the Geneva Convention, and so on. So I think the numbers to me are certainly not excessive, and if I compare them to somewhere like Northern Ireland, whereas I said earlier the military were deployed in support of the civil power, and recognising in that province the size and shape of the Ulster Constabulary, the Royal Ulster Constabulary, then, I think it is difficult to compare the two and say, that it would be an equivalence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we are talking about an area as -- in the assumed facts that you were given in 80(c) of approximately 10.000 square metres for the Krajina -- excuse me, square kilometres, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Square kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I know that it's very difficult to be exact under these circumstances, but given with -- a degree of internally displaced people coming back, and the area just peaking -- taking over for a conflict, can you give us a rough idea of how many people might have been necessary in the law enforcement, bit it military police or civilian police, to bring a degree of security to the area.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I don't want to avoid the question but I don't want to give you a specific answer. I can only say that this province -- this size of terrain, territory we're talking about, is of equivalence to Northern Ireland, and indeed of Kosovo, which is why in my statement I've given roughly the size and shape of those equivalent territories, and each of these locations -- each of these places is, of course, unique, the territory, the size and shape of the villages, the towns, the roads systems. I don't know this part of the Balkans and it is important that I stress that. Therefore, to give you a number, I cannot give you a number. But I do know that in the size -- if one compares the size and shape of Kosovo, Northern Ireland with the sort of numbers that we had in those place, then the -- it is it not an equal comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me talk to you a little bit about the actual planning of these peace support operations that I trust you were involved in with General Garner, and if I can turn your focus to paragraph 55 where you note that: "The planning for a peace support operation as with other operational planning should therefore be guided by a clearly defined strategic end state. And those involved in the planning should include all of the necessary and responsible authorities, ministries, departments, departments of state." Now, explain to us, if you can, that in the area of peace support operations, why people who should -- those people who are responsible should be part of the planning of those peace support operations?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Certainly from my own experiences and a military perspective, we have an expression that says those who plan, implement. Now, this works both ways. It's very easy to come back with a plan in a headquarters back in the United Kingdom, for example, and to be clear about what the intention is, but to actually implement that on the ground in a theatre of operations is much more difficult. On the other hand, to simply be the implementor without understanding what it was and what is the ethos and the ethic that goes behind the planning process puts you in a very difficult situation. So in an ideal situation, if I'm going to be accountable for delivering some sort of success in an operation, it should be me and my staff who plan and implement that operation. And in the context of post-war planning, I would wish to have in my staff, on my staff, representatives of the other non-military players that I alluded. So, for example, in deploying to Washington to begin the post-war plan with Garner, I requested from the United Kingdom and received representatives from the Department of International Development and the Foreign Office, linkages to those departments for the Department for International Development, the man who was given to me was based in New York, and he acted as a link for me whilst I was in Washington, and on my team living with me permanently were members -- two members initially from the Foreign Commonwealth Office. When we deploy to the theatre of operations, the component commanders, the land component commander in particular, was, again attached to his staff, were members of the department for international development, and in the joint headquarters at the three-star level as necessary, other people could be attached to that headquarters, who would be responsible for delivering the non-military parts of that plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cross, may I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would your answer be very short, don't plan a job without involving those who have to do the job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't that true for everything in life? Operations, whether you build a hospital, whether you create a business, whether -- I'm just trying to find out what we have now specifically learned from you and that could I say that this is general wisdom. Don't plan a job and ignore those or don't involve those who have to do the job. That's simply what you're telling us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is true. All I would say that in the environment in which I have operated over the last 30, 40 years, a failure to do that has consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't that true for building a hospital, if you don't involve them that it gets -- it goes wrong? I'm just trying to find out what are just the -- I would say the general lessons we learn in life, and what you're actually saying is that they apply in this field as well. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If that's a fact that's taken off the table and then not part of the Prosecution's case, we will, of course, accept that stipulation from the Prosecution and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's, of course, why we covered the topic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, moving from the planning to the actual execution, if, for instance, the person responsible for this post-war planning was involved with military police and civilian police, would you likewise expect information to be passed to that person who was responsible from the military police or the civilian police, on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the issue here is a clear coherent command and control. Who is -- if I am the commander, when I was involved in these operation, understanding who worked for me, which individuals and which organisations were under my command, and therefore, what would I be held accountable for was clearly important. And those people who worked for me would report back to me on a regular basis as to what was going on, how they intended to executed their part of the plan. For us, the British military, we do that on a daily base sitting around an operational table, going through what is happening, thinking through how we're going to reacts to whatever events are unfurling, and indeed preparing to be proactive in achieving our intent. So I would wanted a regular feedback to me as the commander by the people who I command and who are clearly under my command on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Lastly, General, I just want to cover briefly the issue of pre-planning, and then resources and time available for the pre-planning and implementation. You note in paragraph 38, and in -- you are talking about the Iraq situation. You said. "In my estimation the coherent planning for a post-conflict peace support operation of this magnitude was both late in starting and understaffed." Going to paragraph 80 in the stipulated facts, we noted in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't think they're stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I apologise. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The facts presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- provided, provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, counsellor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 80(e), we're talking about the planning for the peaceful integration going on since 1993, and paragraph (f), the planning for peace support operations following the military liberation of the so-called Krajina region of Croatia begins less than one week prior to Operation Storm. Now, you note in paragraph 30 83 [sic] that that time was insufficient. That's in the last sentence. Can you elaborate on that just a bit. Tell us why you think it's insufficient, and under the circumstances that you have been given in the given facts, how long do you think was necessary for the pre-planning of such an operation as the re-takeover of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Again, maybe unhelpfully, it's difficult for me to give you a time line for an operation that I was not involved with, although I'm aware of it, was not part of the planning process. I said in that part of the -- of my statement that you referred to that for postwar reconstruction of a major world conflict, there had been months, indeed years of the planning, for the post-war reconstruction of Europe. That is a given. And that is at one end of the spectrum, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're talking about after World War II?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I am indeed. The other end of the spectrum, my experience of post-war planning for Iraq, is that Garner is established to take over an office of post-war planning in January 2003. The military campaign to secure Iraq begins in the spring of 2003, that in my estimation, was not sufficient time to enable him to get a coherent plan together and to be able to execute that plan. Rebuilding a nation the size and shape of Iraq, post-military operations, in my estimation should have required a lot longer than that. Now to be fair, in the context of -- or in the context of this court, other departments of state had indeed been doing work for the planning of the reconstruction of Iraq, but Garner, who is in command of this post-war plan, had not been involved in any of those other pieces of work. And, indeed, one of the first things he had to do was to find out what work had been done, meet with those people, and try to discover what planning had been achieved. So I think Garner is at the other end of the spectrum, he is given nowhere near sufficient time to prepare and plan for post-war Iraq. Where does this case fit within there? I would say it is at Garner end of the spectrum, not at the World War II end of the spectrum. I could not tell you whether they needed five weeks or fifteen weeks or twenty weeks, my instinct having understood the facts that you've given to me is that one week is nowhere near sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may have one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Meanwhile, for the record, I already clarify that when Mr. Kehoe and I were competing to be heard, that I said that these were facts presented to the witness on page 40, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, we'll, first of all, carefully consider the positions taken under Rule 94(B) by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I -- I think -- I think the objection is more into the relevance of some portions of the report, and I think that is what the objection would be. utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say -- one second, please, Mr. Kuzmanovic. You would say from questions and answers to the witness, the relevance would emerge.

utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and how the challenge was made and how it was reasoned and that's what we had on our mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My only addition to that is if we can give it to the courtroom deputy, the court officer. utterances.text: And, again, when was the report filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Until -- my calendar is off, I think it is the 20th. I was right the first time, it was the 22nd.

Would you please consider the position of the Prosecution in this respect. We'll meanwhile take a take a break, and we will resume, Mr. Cross, at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed, Mr. Kehoe, that -- that the Prosecution withdraws its objection to admission. Is that ...

utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that just a couple of typos in the record, and this would be at page 30, line 16. It reflects 4.000.727, and if we go back to the particular exhibit it should be 42.000 as opposed to -- and I was quoting. Get the exact exhibit number, it is D1361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the answer of the witness, I think the 42.000 appears, so that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.
