utterances.text: So that's clear and is now on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And there is just one last correction. It's on page 35, line 5. Again, the exhibit says 42.000 and not 32.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in Defence of the court reporter, I'm not sure if I said 32.000 or a mistake, I just want to accurately reflect what the exhibit says, which is 42 -- or approximately 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Kuzmanovic, you had questions for Mr. Cross. Mr. Cross, Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very brief, general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: General, if you could refer your report which we now know is D1624, if you have that front of you?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 80, with various subparagraphs, asked you to consider the following facts in your analysis and conclusions, and two of your conclusions are contained in paragraphs 83 and 84. For my benefit, your conclusions in paragraph 83 and 84 are based in part on your experiences in Kosovo, Cyprus, and Northern Ireland; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: That is correct. I mean, they are based in entirety on those three and post-war Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the assumed facts that you were given in paragraph 80?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to you consider as additional assumed facts that after Operation Storm was concluded there was still a war going on in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, and also to assume that after Operation Storm was concluded there were various pockets of ARSK soldiers still in Sector South to some extent putting some resistance or to some extent hiding. What I'd like to ask you is based upon those assumed the facts, would you agree with me that those additional assumed facts would even further complicate matters that you concluded in paragraphs 83 and 84, in terms of manpower and planning?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Certainly if there are, as I am aware, continuing operations, further operations, that are now being engaged with inside Bosnia, as opposed to the sovereign territory of Croatia, then there is, if you like, the main effort of the military campaign is now moving on to the next phase of this operation. The reality of the fighting that you're referring to means that the -- the rear areas of this operation are still vulnerable in terms of lines of communication and supply and so forth, and securing those lines of communication becomes an important issue, and it isn't easy if people are disrupting your lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The other question, and it will be my last question, General, is your experience in SFOR and KFOR were after essentially hostilities were over; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: That is the case in SFOR and indeed in IFOR; although, for IFOR the previous experiences in Balkans meant that there was no peace to keep. The terminology that was used for IFOR and SFOR, that these were peace enforcement operations; therefore, force would have been used had it been necessary. Of course, during KFOR force was used in terms of the NATO bombing campaign, et cetera. When we actually moved into Kosovo itself, as opposed to the preparations for that and the pre-events that occurred, then there was -- essentially the war was finished, yes. There was no fighting between the warring parties other than the criminality that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So essentially, assuming -- assuming that there were still some pockets of resistance in Sector South in Croatia and that there were active combat operations being conducted in Bosnia during the course after Operation Storm was over, the fact that KFOR and SFOR and IFOR essentially came into play and into their force during a time when combat operations were over is another complicating fact that -- faced implementation and manpower inside Sector South in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I would agree with that sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. You have just, Mr. Cross, answered a question by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who gave as an additional fact to you that various pockets of the ARSK soldiers still had remained in Sector South. How did you understand this information? What -- in what numbers, for example, are you thinking, if you get this information? And would that have any impact on the answers you gave to Mr. Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour, in the sense that if these were relatively isolated incidents, then, from a military point of view, you press on in dealing with what needs to be dealt with, within Bosnia, in this context. If these incidents within the southern part of Croatia were seriously disrupting your ability to conduct operations, then clearly would you have to move assets and deal with that in a much more coherent way, if you like. You would have to put together a much more -- you have a series of contingency operations that you would put into place. So the size and shape of those -- of those continuing operations, yes, indeed, would have an effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you're using the term "southern part of Croatia," whereas Mr. Kuzmanovic said "Sector South." Is that the same for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I realise that Sector South is not completely in its entirety the southern part of Croatia, although it does encompass more than that. I realise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sector South more and or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand it, Sector South is more than just the -- sorry, is less than the whole of the southern half of Croatia. And it includes other operational parts of -- as I understand it, parts of Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you understand it, if I would ask you to mark on a map --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I would not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where Sector South would be, would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in an accurate way. I mean, my understanding is based on my understanding as I deployed to the Balkans in 1995, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a rather general knowledge --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of an area which was called --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Sector South. Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- I just wanted to note for the transcript, and I'm sure it will be corrected, but page 49 lines 8 and 9, there seems to be a -- it might have been probably because I was speaking too fast in the question, and I can't even actually remember that part of the question, but it doesn't make any sense if you look at it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should blame myself perhaps for talking too quickly. I think I asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour I was referring to myself not to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and could you then repeat again the page and line number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 48, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now confusion is total, because I read that you earlier referred to 49, 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I think it applies to both of us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I really have problems exactly to see how we can resolve this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so we're clear, my reference is page 49 lines 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm sure it's recorded so I'm sure Madam Reporter will hopefully figure me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And may I invite you to draw specific attention if you receive or if you have a view of the transcript that it reflects what you said and if not, there's always a way of correcting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will do so Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cross, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What were your instructions in preparing this report? What were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: When I was approached by the counsel to give a -- give a -- my experiences in such operations, I produced a paper, that I believe I sent to yourself as well, which laid out my background and my experiences over the period of my command. Having done that, I wasn't given any instructions on producing the paper. I then met with counsel, talked through those experiences, and they asked me questions in those areas that inevitably were of more relevance to this particular hearing than others, and from that a draft report was produced. I then amended that report in using my own -- my own amendments, if you like, and then sent that report to counsel some time ago but -- in time for them to file it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And who prepared that first draft report?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: The draft report was prepared as a result of the conversations that I had with counsel back in the United Kingdom. They took the notes, they produced the draft, sent it to me. I then went through it in my own time, reflected it, and amended it as I -- as I -- as I tried to ensure that what was being said here was what I believed and using the expressions that I wanted to use. So they had taken extensive notes as a result of initial discussions that I had and used some of the information from the paper that I'd sent them originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, we both tend to speak a little fast --

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I will slow down, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So if I make what seems to you to be inordinately long pauses, it's not an invitation to continue but simply me waiting for the interpreters to catch up with us.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Sure, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you were provided the facts in paragraph 80 on and around 10 June 2009, less than two weeks before this report was filed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes, that's so. I don't know the exact date. I'm very happy to accept your date. Having written my initial -- having written the initial paper, had those discussions, amended the report to reflect my experiences of the various deployments that I had been on, the facts were then given to me, the assumed facts were given to me, and I was asked to reflect on them in the context of what I had said already to see whether these either mitigated against or reinforced some of the points that I had said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you provided your opinions in paragraph 83 through 85, those opinions were based on the specific facts that were provided to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes. The final paragraphs were written as the final draft, really, for summarizing everything that I had done previously and then having been given the facts, the assumed the facts, taking those into consideration, I then wrote the final three, four paragraphs. Five -- five or six paragraphs. And I wrote those at home on my own and then sent the final copy of the report to the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, may I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. This list of facts in which we find in paragraph 80, now were they provided to you before you had these conversations which resulted in a draft report being sent to you; or did you find them listed for the first time in the draft report that was sent to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- in all honesty, Your Honour, I would have to take advice as to dates here. But from my -- the way that I put this together was I was asked to talk through my experiences from the various operations we have spoken about. I was then asked to comment on did I think certain things about the Croatian Operation Storm, how -- how relevant was that, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This was still discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And in saying that, the assumed facts were then given to me, to say, Well, these are the facts as we understand them. In relation to what you have already told us, does that change the way you think, does that reinforce any of the points you were trying to make, or, indeed, detract from any of them? So the assumed facts were given to me after I had prepared quite a lot of this report, which was, of course, and is, of course, simply a report of my own experiences hopefully helping to set a context within which you are considering this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, now, you had these conversations, and at a certain moment you received a draft report, which you then reviewed and you said you would -- well, check whether you would agree or whether you would use other language or -- now, as footnote 12 says: "These facts are as written by General Gotovina's counsel." That means that there must have been a moment in time when you received these facts - and there are quite a number of them - in writing. Now, was that before -- was that during your conversations, your discussions, that you received a written list of facts; or did you found -- find them written only for the first time in the draft report that was sent for review to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, the counsel may wish to comment. But my recollection is, having produced a draft of this report, and having read through it and amended it, in an electronic communication, an e-mail, the assumed facts were passed to me, and I then took those assumed facts, looked at them, and considered them in the light of the report that I had written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, said "having produced a draft of this report," would that include conclusions about the Croatian situation? To say, conclusions and summary of opinion, well, let's say part six of the report. Was that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your first draft was exclusively explaining --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- your experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, then you received this list of facts by e-mail. So, at that point in time, there was no report yet on conclusions on the Croatian situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my recollection of events, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are the witness so we have to rely on -- at this moment, on your recollection. Did you then, on the basis of those facts, draft conclusions as far as Croatia is concerned; or did you receive draft conclusions from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my recollection is that I wrote my own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the key issues were trying to look at this particular operation in relation to the size of the operations in Northern Ireland, geographically, for example, and indeed Kosovo and Iraq, looking at the numbers of people were involved in this, those sorts of issues that those facts were -- looking at them, enabled me to say yes, this is a comparative. It is fair to draw a conclusion from my experience in these places to what was happen on this particular operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, at that time, you then received questions to be dealt with? I mean, you had given your experience. You then received a list of facts about Croatia, and then may I take it that some questions or issues were raised by the Defence at that time? Could you please, in your conclusions, pay attention to A, B, C, D, whatever. Was there a clear --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- there was certainly discussion, but my -- I'm not aware that this paper was amended more than once as a result of having received these assumed facts. I wrote conclusions, there was then discussion both electronically and face to facial on the finalisation of the paper. Nobody -- forgive me because I may be reading something that you're not assessing, but nobody tried to say to me, Can you write this sentence differently, or Could you add something you've not yet put in. As a result of the discussions, I was quite clear what I wanted to include in my report, and I was quite content that having seen the assumed facts, that I could then write the conclusions that I reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- I have no second thoughts on the matter. I just want to have clear on my mind how this report came into being as we find it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just to follow up briefly on that, after you received the assumed facts, did you make any changes to the first 79 paragraphs of the report, or did you only draft the last five or six paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I don't believe I made any changes as a result of seeing the assumed facts. There was nothing that I saw in the assumed facts that made me change what I had already written, because as we said earlier, the vast majority of that was simply relating the events that had occurred in the various deployments and trying to explain the issues of an end state and the strategic and operational levels and so on. So the vast majority of the report written beforehand is simply laying out my experiences. The conclusions that I've written are as a result of seeing the assumed facts, but they did not effect that previous part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you could just look at your report and just so that we are all clear, we're talking about all the way up to page 18 before the section "Provided Facts," that's what you refer to when you are talking to everything before the assumed facts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I think you wanted refer to -- oh, no, it's page 18, and paragraph 80. And that's both the same. That's what's confusing me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- what you have just asked me is correct. I would want to say that, you know, reading the paper, putting it in my own words, amending it to reflect. I wouldn't want to suggest for one minute that I didn't change some of the wording in the early part of the paper before submitting the final draft, reading through it, as I obviously did, trying to assure that it was coherent. I may well have changed some of the sentencing and phrasing, which I would have done having received the facts. My point is that the facts did not change the essence of what I was trying to establish in the first part of the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think I understand you, but just allow me to make sure that -- I don't want to mischaracterise what you've said. You probably would have made some changes throughout these first portions as general edits, let's say, of your draft, but you did not make any specific changes to those portions, because of specific facts that you received; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yeah. That -- that is my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And these facts, and I think you've testified earlier, perhaps a few minutes ago, so I apologise for asking you the same question again, but opinions in paragraphs 83 through 85 were based on those assumed facts that you received that are listed in paragraph 80; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to conclude by recognising the reality of what I had been presented with. I should stress that in writing my initial drafts, I can't remember, to be honest, what those conclusions were, but in concluding there were some basic conclusions, the paragraphs drafted in trying to conclude and summarise what I had tried to say in the first part of the paper. So changing those to reflect the assumed facts that I had been given, trying to draw out key issues from where I was coming from, which had to do with resources, manpower, time-lines, and so on. Trying as I've said both in the introduction to my paper and in my conclusion, particularly at paragraph 85, that I - very clearly - am not -- was not part of this operation, I was not there on the ground, I make no judgement at all on -- on those sorts of aspect, and that's what I've tried to summarise in that particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if I could just invite you -- I don't want to belabour this point, but I'm -- I apologise if I'm a little confused. If you look at paragraphs 81 and 82 at page 21 of your report, under the section -- under the heading "Conclusions and Summary of Opinion," paragraphs 81 and 82 are essentially the general conclusions of what is contained in your report from paragraphs 1 to 79; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: That's correct. And they would have been written in that initial -- when I wrote the initial conclusions, they would have been the way that I had tried to summarise what I had put in the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 83 you give an opinion, "Given the facts provided to me in paragraph 80," and then you say the same thing in paragraphs 84. So it's that those two paragraphs are opinions based solely on the assumed facts given to you?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if these facts were not accurate or if you were given different facts, it would therefore follow that your conclusions would also be different; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. Well, I should say, if I may, it would depend on what those new facts were. But in principle I understand what you are saying and I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. You mention both in your report and earlier today that the criminality that occurred, for example, in Iraq, was not unusual or unexpected. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, would you have expected the troops of General Franks to commit crimes in Iraq, following the military operation?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: No, sir. If you are distinguishing between the troops under the command of General Franks as opposed to what the Iraqi people themselves were doing, I would not have expected them to be involved and engaged in that criminality themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were you aware, sir, that this Chamber has received evidence that soldiers involved in retaking the territory were involved in a significant amount of crimes committed in the area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to the word "significant."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well -- yes. What makes an amount significant, what not. Let's say was involved certainly not in a sporadic way. An amount not of a -- certainly not of a sporadic nature. Would you please answer the question? Well, Mr. Kehoe, of course, this witness has been fed with a long list of facts on which, whether established or not, whether they're complete or not, whether they're -- what's the basis for the selection is still to be seen. So, therefore, Mr. Hedaraly now puts other facts. You would say it's -- you have -- you object to putting to him that it is a significant. I could imagine - I don't know whether that's true or not - that Mr. Hedaraly would object to some of the facts as presented here as well, but they were the facts given to the expert. I think I have sized it down slightly, and invite witness to answer the question. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll let Mr. Kehoe go --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if counsel wants to say assume X/Y facts, as he has done before with an expert and as Mr. Kuzmanovic did, that's the proper cross-examination of a witness, but to postulate that there has been a significant amount presented to this Chamber, we take issue with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well -- and you may -- yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, and if Mr. Hedaraly, as Your Honour put it, would object to some facts as presented, he could have done so in a filing opposing expert's report and we could have all had knowledge of that prior to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the structure of the report, you put certain facts to the witnesses, to fully litigate whether that is complete or not would come close to final argument, Mr. Kuzmanovic, which is certainly not something one would seek in preparing this expert report, and cross-examination of this witness. You may have forgotten about the question already. Let's go back to it. And ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm comfortable with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may also, I would like to say, as we go into this period, that I absolutely understand that the facts that were presented to me as a result of my initial writing of my views on these deployments were undoubtedly facts that were there to draw out certain lessons and to reinforce some of the points that I made, and I absolutely understand that there were maybe other facts that may -- would led me to say other things or draw other conclusions. As I said at the beginning of paper, my intent here is to try to assist the Court as a whole in understanding what it is like to be involved in these post-conflict operations. So I have no problem with the tenant of the question. That said, I also would like to say, if I may, having served in the Balkans three times that, and I touched on this slightly earlier before, when we look at the competency of military organisations we can talk about their equipment, we can talk about their understanding of warfare. For me, the key issue, not just in the Balkans but everywhere else, is what the British military talk about as being the moral component of fighting power. It's about leadership. It's about ethic. It's about understanding the Law of Armed Contact, the Geneva Convention. It's about how you conduct operations. And in first-world armies, American, British Armies and so on, we take that extremely seriously. There are, unfortunately, still occasions when that goes wrong. We can look at that in terms of Iraq or other operations around the world. My own experience is the Balkans make it very clear to me that the moral component, constituent moral component of all the forces engaged in operations in the Balkans was nowhere what I would want to have seen in any military organisation that I served with. So the fact that there were -- whether they are considered to be with respect to everybody significant or insignificant, the fact that there are so-called soldiers within these various armed factions in the Balkans doing bad things, criminality, ethnic cleansing, killings, and so on, I am certainly aware of that because I saw the evidence of it, the results of it. What actually happened in Operation Storm, I can't comment on because I wasn't engaged in that operation, but I am certainly aware that lots of bad things went on on all sides over the whole period of the operations in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, if -- if the crimes that were committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm were committed mainly by the forces that retook the territory, isn't that a fact that would have been relevant for you to know in coming to your conclusions about resources and so on?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: It would -- it would certainly be -- if the fact that you are presenting, that the majority were, the size and shape and scale of those was made clear, it would be an issue to which, in phrasing my conclusions, I may wish to make an adjustment one way or the other. The -- I think in the context of what was happening, and I think again I shouldn't be leading you where you are trying to take me, but in the context of what was happening if there is an assumption that these things were going on because they were part of the operation, they were ordered to happen and so forth, understanding and knowing that as facts would clearly have -- have affected the way that I tried to draw my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that if this Trial Chamber found that the military operation was conducted in a manner to remove the Serb civilians from the area, that would also be a fact that would have affected your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I mean, if the Trial Chamber found -- I mean, we're still in trial. I object to the premise of if -- if the counsel wants to ask -- excuse me, I need to change microphones here a moment. If counsel wants to ask hypothetical situations like that for the witness, that's fine. But positing something about what the Trial Chamber found or didn't find, that's why we're here and I object to the form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please rephrase, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. General, if a military operation was conducted in a manner to remove the Serb civilian population from the area, would that also have been a fact that would have affected your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I think it would be -- I'm not sure that it would have affected the conclusions markedly, in that what I was trying to draw in my paper, what I'm trying to assist the Court in understanding as a whole, is the chaotic nature of post-war operations and the inherent nature of that chaos, and the things that flow from it. However hard and well intentioned the forces apply their military power post-operations. So for example, whilst I am very conscious of what happened in Kosovo and indeed Baghdad and indeed Northern Ireland, in those phases I'm quite clear that there was no intent, within the KFOR chain of command, within the US/UK chain of command, the coalition chain of command, or indeed within the UK chain of command in Northern Ireland, to bring about those things. Your comment to my mind relates back to the end state, the strategic end state, what was trying to be achieved here. And if you were to present to me a strategic end state that made it quite clear that the military campaign was about the sort of thing you are alluding to, it would effect the -- if there was no intention to bring order and structure to post-war operations, then that clearly would have affected what had I would want to say. If there was no intention to do that, then my facts are almost irrelevant. If there was a clear intent to do that, then the numbers of people, the planning processes to bring order post-Operation Storm, my conclusion, having been given the facts that I have been given, was that that planning process, those resources and the other points that I make, were insufficient in order to bring about that order post-war. Does that -- is that clear? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think I was with you just until the end. Let me just read it, and I will see if it is clear to me.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, I understood very well. Let me move to a specific conclusion that you drew based on the facts you were given and that is the one about lack of available resources, and you find that in paragraph 84 at page 22 of your report. And I just want to be clear that the facts that you are referring to here are the numbers of military and civilian policemen. The numbers that were provided to you that are found in paragraphs (w) through (z) of the assumed facts. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The numbers that you referred to were the numbers that I took into consideration. And for complete clarity, that is why when, as a result of additional evidence that was presented that -- the numbers in paragraph (z) were then -- I was then told that they were more than 4 or 500. They were the 7 or 800 we referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear, that change in number did not affect your conclusion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about resources one of the terms that you used that was also mentioned in direct examination is this idea of boots on the ground or more specifically the number of soldiers per square kilometre tasked with providing security. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you gave some examples, based on your previous experiences. And, of course, I understand that -- your evidence to be that these numbers by themselves are not -- not an automatic scale to apply. They depend on circumstances. But the examples that you gave was that 1.67 soldier per square kilometre was sufficient in Operation Banner. Whereas 0.34 were not sufficient in Iraq and you also gave 4.5 per kilometre squared for Kosovo. All of this is at page -- paragraph 70 to 72 of your report. Were you aware that there were UNPROFOR troops on the ground in the Krajina before and after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I was aware that UNPROFOR were in that region. I was not aware of actual deployment locations in relation to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 7360. And it will come up on your screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one minor correction for counsel. I think we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel switch to the other microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry. I think for the clarity in the -- in the record so -- because there has been talk about UNCRO. We're talking about UNCRO at that point as opposed to UNPROFOR which is in Bosnia, and so the witness doesn't get confused between UNCRO in Croatia and UNPROFOR in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine. I will just show the document to the witness, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If that changes your answer at all, General, please --

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: No, I should have corrected it myself. Counsel is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You see here, General, this is dated February 1995, and you see at the top there that -- I mean, I'm going to give an approximate figure that 90 per cent of the complete mission are soldiers and policemen. And then if you go to the Sector South and Sector North, you see that there were 4.614 personnel in Sector South, and based on the top figures that most of those, we can assume, are soldiers and policemen. And just so you know as well, the area of the Split Military District that was under the control of General Gotovina during Operation Storm, is roughly 4.000 square kilometres. That can be found at P482. So now you can see, General, that that is roughly one UN -- that's a soldier or policeman per square kilometre. And my question to you is: If the purpose had been to bring security to the area, wouldn't you consider it logical to use these UN forces to assist in providing security?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: The -- one of the points I was making earlier of the utility of military, non-military, international organisations, non-governmental aid organisations, from a personal point of view, in my view, every available asset should be used to bring about stability post-war operations. Now, that is not the case in every deployment that I have been on, but the principle -- in principle my answer to your question is: If it is possible to do so, use every asset that you have available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can tender 65 ter 7360 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in theory I don't have an objection. If we just MFI it, I can take a look at it at the break and then just give the position --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seems to be the whole of the document, a fact sheet, 14th of February, which lists only the -- well, the authorised strength, and the actual strength being approximately 12 per cent lower. And apparently the numbers, Mr. Hedaraly, presents the actual strength, because adding them up, brings us to the figure of 44.547.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I guess my question is I thought this was a multi-page document. Is it just this sheet? Well, then I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will become Exhibit P2601.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, General, you were not -- in the facts provided to you, and correct me if I'm wrong, you were not provided the number of Croatian soldiers who remained in the area after Operation Storm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now put up on the screen 65 ter 1231, which is a report by General Cervenko of 21 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General Cervenko, at the time, was the Chief of Staff of the Croatian army. And this is his report on Operation Storm that will come up in a few seconds. I just want to draw your attention to a few -- few portions of this. You can see the heading to satisfy yourself that the document is sent to the president of Croatia and is a report on Operation Storm. If we go to the second page of this document, you will see a -- after the list of items it says: "The total of 127.000 members of HV, military police, and MUP have taken part of the attack for liberation of the occupied Croatian territory, Operation Storm." So just keep that number in mind for now, 127.000. And I don't want to confuse you. This is the entire operation, so it is both Sector South and Sector North, so th 10.000 square kilometres, not the 4.000. Just so we are clear.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to page 10 of this document in the English, item VI. I think it's page 7 in the B/C/S but -- I'm fairly sure. If we go down you see and it say there: "At the moment, there was 30.000 demobilised HV members."

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now let me just ask you, you said just earlier that you would use every possible asset to try to secure the territory. Would 30.000 soldiers be an asset that you would try to use to try to secure the territory?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I understand -- the understand the line. And I would think my response would be yes, recognising -- and I think the issue would be whether these were -- first of all, who was in overall command of this operation, were all of these assets under the command of that person, did he have full command and control of them? Now, Your Honour, we could get into a very difficult discussion about command here, because in -- from a UK point of view, we will have garrisons and administrative districts commanded by various people who are not under the command of an operational commander who happens to live and operate in that same territory. So if I may give an example, I commanded a brigade in the United Kingdom. My brigade lived in a part of the country that was under the command of another brigadier whose responsibilities were to administer that area of the country. So in this context, if all of these people that you have presented are clearly under the command and under a single coherent command and they are all available to be used in achieving the post-conflict stability, then in principle my answer is yes. Now, I caveat that slightly, in that in having been given the assumed facts that I was given by counsel, and going back to our earlier conversation, I had discussions with them about what that meant, how did it operate. In the short time in which you have given to me, I'm responding as honestly and as positively as I can do, but there may be all sorts of other aspects to this that I am not aware. So I must caveat my response in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I completely understand your answer, General. If you were to assume that -- and I know that was not one of the facts given to you, but if you were to assume that General Gotovina did have control, military control of that territory, then that would change your answer?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Again, I must be clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- Mr. Hedaraly, I think that the witness explained that it depends on command, availability, a lot of the circumstances. What do you say, maybe yes, maybe no. That's more or less your answer, depends on the circumstances. Now to take out one of them, and then ask him, Would, under those circumstances, that ignores the other caveats, there seems to be even perhaps more caveats than there is answer. I'm not blaming you for that, not in any way, Mr. Cross but it makes no sense to continue questioning and to some extent ignoring what the witness told us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So we had 127.000 in the operation. 30.000 at the time of this report were demobilized. If we go to the second page of the document -- the next page, sorry, of this document, you see at the top there, it says: "Sufficient forces were left in the areas of responsibility of Military District to guard the borders and control territory behind the borders?" So now we have 97.000 remaining forces. Now let's just assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- could you explain the number, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was looking at 127.000 minus 30.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed the 30. And isn't it true that at least this Chamber has had some evidence that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's what I was going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- forces were not necessarily on the territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was my hypothetical, Your Honour, that I was going into. I started by saying let's just assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- that a number and I was going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or double the numbers. Let's just assume that they are wrong and that they are the double. What about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was going provide a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, this witness doesn't know anything -- one thing is clear: Feed this witness with the information or the facts that would encourage him to lead him to the answers you would most likely want to hear from him. That's an exercise. We could go on with that for days and weeks, and finally, you might get 25 per cent of the answers you would like to have. Let's -- let's not -- try to avoid that, Mr. Hedaraly. If you are saying 127.000 minus 30.000 demobilised, then of course one of the assumptions where there may be good reasons to believe that that assumption is not true would be that all these soldiers were still on Croatian territory, or in Sector South. And -- well, I'm not going to stop you immediately, but I think I explained to you that that might not really assist the Chamber. But perhaps I have misunderstood your line of questioning, so perhaps I should be more patient. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I rise only because there's an interpretation or, I should say, a translation issue in the document itself which may be of some relevance certainly to the witness with respect to the sentence that was quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we have such an issue, then I would seek your assistance or at least any native speaking person to read the line and then, of course, we'll see whether the translation would be the same approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will begin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: From the first sentence in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the page on the screen. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't received translation but could be that the interpreters were waiting to hear the whole of the line. But if you slowly restart, Mr. Misetic, then -- and let's -- let's wait getting upset for a few seconds now and then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] "In the areas of responsibility of the Military Districts, enough forces were left to guard the border and control the area in depth." [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly. The translation we received now is the control the territory in depth which from what I understand has a self military meaning. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I -- I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the translation we received now is the "control the territory in depth," which, from what I understand, has a specific military meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just -- briefly, Mr. President. I understand the Chamber's guidance. This whole report was prepared and provided based on facts given by the Gotovina Defence to the expert for him to come to certain conclusions. I understand and I will not go through the entire Prosecution case and give that the witness, but I think that it is only fair for us as well to present some facts. And if I had finished my question, Your Honour would have seen that I was trying to present a reasonable assumption of the -- in the assumption -- in the hypothetical that I was making. That's simply what I wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it may not come as a surprise that if, as the witness did, if you give your expert opinion based on certain facts, that relevant changes in those facts will result in different answers. There is, as such, apart from that perhaps you want to demonstrate it in one or two instances, but there is, as such, I think, no doubt about that. But I would not prevent you from demonstrating that in relation to one or two examples. But let's not go through the whole of it, and, further, if you give different facts or other facts, perhaps also try to remain at not too much a distance from the evidence, as the party understood it, the Chamber has received. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: While we're here, can you clarify for us what it would mean to control the territory in the depth?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: And I -- again, I think from my perspective and my experience as military words like "control" -- words like "control," you know, do have meanings. We used words like "destroy," "defeat," "control," whatever, and they carry certain nuances that after 30 or 40 years in the military you instinctively understand, but it is quite difficult to define them really. And in the context of the sufficient forces controlling in depth, that would depend for me -- my reaction to that is that would depend on the circumstances on the ground. So if things are relatively quiet and there's no huge amounts of disruption, forces can control in the sense of keep a track of people's movements, be able to deal with individual incidents in a relatively coherent way; but if the terrain is -- or the territory has got a lot of incidents going on, there are lots of people moving around, there's a lot of banditry and criminality, then establishing control is a completely different picture. So I -- although, again, I stress I'm here to try and assist the Court in the round and I hear what you are saying again, it's, again, difficult to know who are these 30.000 or 97.000, what is their professionalism, are they professional soldiers who are garrisoning the towns, are they under clear command and control, are they volunteers, have been in the military for a long time, am I able to give them orders, what is happening around me in the context of this territory, all of which you -- the Court may be able to establish with clarity and hold to account the commander on the ground at the time. I cannot comment on whether or not that is established. You can establish that or not. So, I'm trying to be helpful but I think I don't think I can say anything more unless there is something specific you would like to tease out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, that's fine. I think the -- the only point that I wanted to make, and I think that that's what you've said, and the subject of the caveats that you have mentioned earlier for the 30.000 soldiers, if there were any available soldiers on the territory subject to the command and control caveat that you have raised before, those would be assets that would be want to employ in securing the territory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Yes, with the caveats and -- alongside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. No, that's understood. Now, you also provided information about a number of civilian police officers, and I asked you earlier to assume that a number of these crimes were committed by military personnel. If that were the case, if soldiers successful in retaking an area committed crimes, in your experience, what could civil police officers do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Again, I can only put this in the context of the UK military procedures. Soldiers are subject to civil law and military law. Within the British military, we have military policemen and military lawyers who are part of the command structure. So if soldiers under my command or a British military command were involved in criminality, the commander of the force has military policemen and a judicial system that can conduct the initial investigation. Depending upon the circumstance, in the United Kingdom, for example, very quickly, that might be handed over to the civil authority to deal with. In places like Germany, where we were based under a status of forces agreement, there would be procedures with the German legal system and the British legal system, and the niceties of that I don't understand, but in some cases, the -- the case would be handed over again to civil -- civil authority, or in other cases the military person who had committed a crime or was being accused of committing a crime would be held in British military prison whilst the court case proceeded, may even be brought back to the United Kingdom for that to be brought to trial. On operations, similar would apply. In some cases the military would deal with the issue if it was under military law, but in serious civilian criminality terms, they would be passed over to the civil authority. And I should stress, if I may, that the military commander does not have authority over the civil police system, and he does not have authority to interfere with the military police and the military legal system in conducting what it needs to happen. So the commander cannot step in and say, I do not want that man to be charged if he has been found doing something and has been caught and has been brought to court, the commander has to step away from that while justice is conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that is based all of this on your understanding of the UK military system and civilian system; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: So if I can give, if it's helpful, to give an example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just intervene. I think we have heard for hours and hours, evidence what was the competence of the civilian police and under what circumstances, even if we would have a soldier as a suspect, whether they -- we could intervene. Now, in the last answer we have heard an explanation about the British system, which might be -- one thing I know that the British system in many respects differs from continental European systems, whether it's police or whether it's court systems. We have now dealt with status of forces agreement, in Germany, most likely NATO status of forces agreements, with additional agreements, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I did not want to interrupt the witness, Mr. President, and that's why -- I simply wanted to clarify which that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- you don't have any knowledge of the Croatian military or civilian system?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination. General, thank you very much for your assistance and for answering the questions. I'm just reminded, if I could tender 65 ter 1231, the document on the screen, and then I will formally conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2602.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Has the cross-examination triggered any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have one or more questions for you. Let me first find the relevant portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to ask you the following. Mr. Kuzmanovic added two facts to the list of facts and asked whether it would further complicate matters. The first fact would be that after Operation Storm was concluded, that there was still a war going on in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, looking at the list of facts that were put to you, and I'm referring to page 20, under T and U, that the VRS organises military operations against General Gotovina's forces in Bosnia, and that on or about the 12th of August, General Mladic launches a counteroffensive against HV forces never the Croatian-Bosnian border, would that first fact not already, in your view, having been among those facts that you had considered in drawing your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: It was, Your Honour, in that in looking at what needed to be done and the numbers and the resources that were available, recognising that there were events like that happening. Now, again, I think it's important to recognise I'm not aware of how that particular event unfurls. I had within it, assumed that this is, if you like, a regular army counteroffensive. This is not insurgents, this is not banditry, this is a military counteroffensive, and that in the follow-on facts that were presented, General Gotovina defends the line and then continues with his operational -- his operations -- his operation Southern Sweep and so on. So it is a fact that I was aware of, but in the context of what is going on in post-war operations, the post-conflict, reconstruction, and trying to restore order in the main part of this area of operations, this, to me, is part of the follow-on. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Is that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand your answer. At the same time that was not the fact that was submitted to you by Mr. Kuzmanovic, because what he gave you as a new fact or perhaps not a new fact is that a war was going on in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina. Which I understood, Mr. Kuzmanovic, that this already demonstrates how fragile these kind of assumptions are, that it was the war in which the same forces that were involved in Operation Storm, at least some of them were involved, but now across the border the war continuing there. And that is something I thought was already reflected --

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- under T and U.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the second fact which was new was the pockets of RSK soldiers of which, I think you later said it very much depends on what it is, is it -- so, therefore, you quickly answered that matters became more complex, whereas, for one of the facts you had already considered, so for that reason it could not have become more complex, because it was already part of the facts; and the other one was so vague to understand what it actually meant, that it would be difficult to draw the conclusion that it would -- makes matters more complex. Would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I understand your point, Your Honour, I think my -- in responding to the way the question was phrased, if these are major operations, large casualties are being caused, there is this war that's going on in Bosnia and is beginning to incur across the borders and is now beginning to take my mind -- draw my attention to it, then yes it becomes more complex. But again, I do understand your point, and it is -- it is relevant in terms of the size and shape of what these things are, and if -- if they were significant, they would make the attempt to bring order to this region much more difficult. My understanding was that these were relatively small occurrences, but if that were not to be the case it would make it more complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question, and perhaps also a bit of a general kind, is your conclusions in your report are based on your experience, Kosovo, Iraq, Northern Ireland, and the facts that were given to you in relation to Croatia, facts which were presented to you and were not verified by you, would you agree with me that whether these conclusions can be drawn entirely depends on to what extent the comparison between the Croatian situation and the Kosovo situation, Northern Ireland situation, et cetera, would be of a similarity which would allow for drawing conclusions of -- based on the experience in the other areas?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: I would, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to give you an example. Would, for example, would it for you make a difference comparing with Iraq that from what I understand after Iraq had been militarily taken, that there was no still-functioning government anymore which had to be fully re-established. The old governmental system having collapsed; whereas in Croatia one might think of Croatia still having a government but had it retaken certain territory, on which it could well, extend or re-build on the basis of existing governmental institutions to that area. Would, for example, such a difference, would that be relevant for you, and I'm not asking whether it would change your conclusions, but would that have an impact, an important impact, on considering the situation of the type of operations you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. If I may just expand on those. I think Iraq is, of course, a military occupation, and under international law certain things flow from that, and therefore the responsibility of commanders in Iraq are different than responsibilities within the sovereign territory where there is a functioning government. So Iraq is at one end of that spectrum, if you like. Northern Ireland was part of the sovereign territory of the United Kingdom. In the earlier 1970s there was a period of time there were what were termed to be "no go areas" within certain cities of Northern Ireland, and under a military operation called Motor Man we cleared those areas to re-establish the sovereign rule of law in those areas. So as I understand this operation within Croatia, and as you've explained it, this is the sovereign territory of Croatia, and the military commander, having conducted a military operation, it is then the responsibility of the sovereign government, the civil power, and the ministries to re-establish every aspect of post-conflict situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't want specifically focus on the difference between Iraq and Croatia, but I just wanted to highlight one of the circumstances which might have an impact on the conclusions of how much the problems, huge and complex problems, you faced everywhere, to what extent comparing them is -- is be done on a one-to-one basis.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Sure. And I did try to say in the report that you cannot just pick out the circumstances of one operation and implant it into another. They are always unique. You always have to assess it on a one-to-one basis. So everything that I have explained in my report, which lays out my experiences, I would be the first to acknowledge may or may not be applicable in this particular operation, at this particular time, in the circumstances that the commander on the ground found himself. Nonetheless, there were some underlying issues in terms of how long did he have to prepare, how much resource did he have, what was the size of the operation, what was going on in that operation. Some of those things, I think, are applicable in every sort of operation that we have been involved with over these last 20 or 30 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the general message seems to be don't underestimate what it takes --

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In such kind of operations.

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Absolutely. And if I may just add, if you want to work on the basis that everything will go well, plan A is we will not have a problem here. A good military commander or a good organisation planning this process has always got to have some sort of reserve. Okay, if that doesn't happen what then do we do? And if you don't have a plan B, or indeed a plan C, and if we don't actually recognise in reality whatever contingency plans you've, you always have to adapt them to suit the circumstances, then you can run into trouble very quickly. So you must not underestimate. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As doctors have to do, as companies have to do, as --

utterances.speaker: TIMOTHY CROSS
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Cross, in the beginning I said it is no disrespect of positions and titles, perhaps I should have added ranks. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no more witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a few procedural matters which the Chamber would like to deal with before the recess. At the same time, the Chamber needs some additional time to discuss a few matters and to prepare for them. To some extent, they are related also to scheduling issues for after the recess. I suggest to the parties that we will adjourn for the day, and have a hearing tomorrow relatively short, not necessarily starting at 9.00 in the morning which would give additional time for the Chamber to deliberate on certain matters and to clear our desks before the recess. Let me first hear whether there's any objection to -- if the Chamber would decide to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We, of course, have no objection. If I can just put one issue on the table, and I haven't talked to our client yet, but he is shaking his head, if we have procedural matters, can they be excused or certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They, of course, they are -- I mean, a request for a week not sitting is of course a procedural matter but, of course, might have a direct effect. When we are discussing procedural matters, and if we're not hearing any evidence and not thoroughly discussing on admissibility of evidence, then, of course, the accused always have -- I wouldn't say have a right, but if they waive their right to be present, under those circumstances the Chamber would easily accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think I'm speaking for my colleagues that they have all agreed that they will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I apologise. Your Honour, for my part we needed to see Mr. Cermak tomorrow before the recess, and I was at one stage trying to book a DU visit in the morning, but then I was quite satisfied if we were going to be sitting and he was going to be here, because then I could speak to him here and hand to him certain documents before the recess starts, so I -- I don't have a Croatian speaker with me on the bench, and I'm not sure if I speak to him he will fully understand, but I know this is being interpreted, whether I need to hand certain documents to him tomorrow, and it may be better if he comes to court and then that can serve that process. It will be easier than trying to fix things for the DU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am not fully familiar with all the practical difficulties that creates, but you have put it now on the record now. So Mr. Cermak would have a good reason to come, if he wants to see the documents you want to hand out to him. If he doesn't wanted to see them then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the translators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow, 24th of July, most likely for one session only, to start at 11.00, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 24th day of July, 2009, at 11.00 a.m.
